body.text: Nations are used to diplomacy in the embassy. But in the South China Sea, consequential exchanges between states also occur on board vessels – or between them.

In contested waters, conflict prevention should commence when ships come face to face at sea. Commanding officers and radio operators may only have a few minutes to communicate their position, respond to radio challenges, interpret the other vessel’s movements and decide how far an encounter could go without further intensifying tensions. During these critical moments, how they communicate influences whether the encounter de-escalates or develops into a crisis.

One policy that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member states should seek to adapt would be to integrate a “Diplomatic Communication Exercise”, or DIPLOMEX, into existing bilateral and multilateral interoperability exercises among coast guard counterparts and their regional partners.

Diplomatic communication, in this context, means expressing a state’s intent and clarifying actions while responding to another state vessel with restraint and resolve, within the authority of the frontline personnel on board.

Countries such as Australia could also support this kind of capability development as part of its expanding maritime security cooperation with Southeast Asia towards a safer and more stable Indo-Pacific region.
Diplomatic communication, in this context, means expressing a state’s intent and clarifying actions while responding to another state vessel with restraint and resolve.

CUES, or the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea, provides procedures for safe and professional exchanges between naval ships and aircraft during unplanned encounters. Its scope does not extend to coast guard and other maritime law enforcement vessels.

Regional coast guards have been advancing the Southeast Asia Protocol of Engagement at Sea for Coast Guard and Maritime Law Enforcement, or SEA-PEACE as a product of the ASEAN Coast Guard Forum. In June 2026, the Philippine Coast Guard and Indonesia’s Bakamla RI discussed a trial implementation of SEA-PEACE. The meeting also affirmed continued patrol cooperation between the two maritime security agencies.
DIPLOMEX could complement CUES and SEA-PEACE by providing an avenue to practise diplomatic communication under pressure, with state vessels pursuing distinct objectives.

Imagine two coast guard ships coming into close proximity, each carrying competing instructions. Under the guidance of their respective commanding officers, radio operators would rehearse how to clarify intentions and issue appropriate warnings without unnecessary escalation.

DIPLOMEX is about exercising firmness with discipline. The training could simulate actions that commonly lead to heightened tensions at sea, including a misunderstood manoeuvre, an aggressive radio warning, the use of water cannons, or a deliberate attempt to obstruct another state vessel. Tensions should be high. Every second intensifies pressure.

International law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), should guide how coast guard and maritime law enforcement personnel communicate the legal basis of their actions and responses.
Evaluators should assess how commanding officers and radio operators pursue their missions amid tense situations at sea and recognise when an encounter needs to be elevated to higher authorities.

DIPLOMEX could initially be incorporated into existing joint exercises, with participating agencies assigned opposing objectives. A pilot within Southeast Asia’s maritime domain would allow them to assess its operational value before considering broader use in future engagements.

There are limits to what diplomatic communication can accomplish. DIPLOMEX cannot resolve competing sovereignty claims or guarantee cooperation from another state vessel. Its purpose is more immediate: to equip frontline personnel to communicate in ways that build confidence and manage escalation risks while preserving their mandates.

As SEA-PEACE moves towards trial implementation, ASEAN member states have a timely opportunity to consider how DIPLOMEX could reinforce the protocol by strengthening the ability of coast guards and their regional partners to manage the operational realities of contested waters.
More than improving safety in maritime encounters, DIPLOMEX would give commanding officers and radio operators the composure and judgement to communicate diplomatically during volatile situations.
